FINDING_ID: VC_F001
SEVERITY: 0.78
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.64
DESCRIPTION: `verify_record()` can report success for a record inside an invalid chain suffix because `_verify_single()` validates only the immediate predecessor hash, not that the predecessor record itself is valid. This is distinct from the already-known “standalone validity check” issue at a general level: here the concrete failure mode is that if record `i-1` is internally corrupted but its stored `chain_hash` is left untouched, record `i` can still verify successfully because `_verify_single(i, ...)` trusts `self._records[i-1]["chain_hash"]` as the expected predecessor anchor. The API therefore permits local verification results that are not prefix-sound.
PROPOSED_FIX: Make `verify_record(index)` verify the full prefix `0..index` or require the caller to supply a trusted predecessor digest and verify transitively. At minimum, document that single-record verification is only meaningful when all prior records have already been verified.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F002
SEVERITY: 0.74
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.57
DESCRIPTION: `head()` exposes a live mutable alias to internal chain state, unlike the `records`/`epochs` properties which at least copy the outer list. A caller can do `chain.head()["sealed_body"]["seq"] = 999` or mutate nested payload/metadata through the returned object and silently corrupt in-memory state. This is a separate API escape hatch from the already-known shallow-copy issues on `records` and `epochs`.
PROPOSED_FIX: Return a deep copy from `head()`, or an immutable view/dataclass. If mutability is intentionally exposed, rename/document it as unsafe internal access rather than “return the latest record”.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F003
SEVERITY: 0.66
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.41
DESCRIPTION: `_normalize_timestamp()` accepts special ISO 8601 values with UTC offsets containing seconds or fractional seconds, then silently normalizes them to whole-second `Z` form. That means syntactically different but valid timestamps like `2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00:30` or offsets with sub-minute precision can be accepted and collapsed into a normalized UTC instant without any policy check. For an audit format claiming RFC 3339 UTC output, this is too permissive and may admit timestamps outside the intended profile.
PROPOSED_FIX: Enforce a strict input profile explicitly: accept only RFC 3339 timestamps with `Z` or `±HH:MM`, reject offsets with seconds/fractions, and reject anything that cannot round-trip under that profile.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F004
SEVERITY: 0.63
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.36
DESCRIPTION: `_digest_bytes()` accepts digests with surrounding non-empty hex payload after `sha256:` but does not reject embedded whitespace once the prefix check passes. For example, `sha256: abcd...` reaches `bytes.fromhex`, which tolerates spaces between hex byte pairs in some forms. That makes the accepted digest syntax looser than the emitted canonical format and can permit non-canonical persisted digests to verify. This is distinct from the known “any length” and uppercase issues: it is a text-format normalization gap.
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate digests with a strict regex such as `^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$` before decoding, and reject any whitespace or non-canonical form.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F005
SEVERITY: 0.71
FLAW_CLASS: 4
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.53
DESCRIPTION: The module exports low-level Merkle helpers (`rfc9162_merkle_root`, `rfc9162_inclusion_proof`, `rfc9162_verify_inclusion`) but not the leaf-hash convention as part of a stable public contract, even though correctness depends on passing raw `chain_hash` bytes, not prehashed leaves. This creates an interoperability trap: an external caller can reasonably prehash leaves before calling the public helpers, producing silently wrong roots/proofs. The docstrings mention “raw leaf data,” but the API surface still invites misuse because the naming does not distinguish leaf payloads from leaf hashes.
PROPOSED_FIX: Rename parameters and functions to make the contract explicit, e.g. `*_from_leaf_data`, or expose a public `rfc9162_leaf_hash()` and document the exact leaf domain. Better, wrap the Merkle API at the chain level and avoid exporting ambiguous low-level helpers.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F006
SEVERITY: 0.69
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.49
DESCRIPTION: `verify_chain()` does not validate that records are contiguous in list position versus declared chain length beyond per-record `seq == index`. Because epochs are verified after records and only against `self._records[:record_count]`, a chain can contain structurally nonsensical trailing garbage records after a valid prefix and still yield valid earlier epochs and valid inclusion proofs for prefix members. This is not just the known lack of schema validation; it is missing an explicit notion of “authoritative head” or sealed extent. The structure has no way to state “only first N records are committed” versus “entire list is committed.”
PROPOSED_FIX: Introduce a committed-head concept, e.g. signed/sealed chain metadata or epoch binding to head `chain_hash`, and make verification distinguish committed prefix from uncommitted trailing records.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F007
SEVERITY: 0.61
FLAW_CLASS: 8
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.34
DESCRIPTION: The documentation states “Epoch inclusion: RFC 9162-compliant Merkle trees over sealed epochs allow compact inclusion proofs for any individual record,” but the public low-level verifier `rfc9162_verify_inclusion()` is generic over arbitrary leaf data and does not explain that chain-level proofs use `chain_hash` bytes as leaves. The documentation therefore omits the concrete proof object semantics needed for independent implementations. This is narrower than the already-known epoch/proof design flaws: even within the current design, the proof format is underspecified.
PROPOSED_FIX: Specify the proof object contract precisely in module docs: leaf value = raw bytes of record `chain_hash` digest, proof steps are bottom-up sibling subtree roots, root format is `sha256:<hex>` at chain API level and raw bytes at low-level API level.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: VC_F008
SEVERITY: 0.65
FLAW_CLASS: 6
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.39
DESCRIPTION: `main()` dispatch assumes every handler returns an `int`, but several handlers call code paths that can raise uncaught filesystem exceptions (`PermissionError`, `OSError`, short reads, broken pipes on stdout). For a persistence CLI intended for audit workflows, this means operational failures surface as Python tracebacks rather than stable exit semantics. This is separate from the already-known JSON parse and malformed-structure issues.
PROPOSED_FIX: Wrap top-level handler execution in `try/except OSError, json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError` as appropriate, print concise diagnostics to stderr, and return nonzero exit codes without tracebacks for expected operational failures.
VERIFIED: TRUE

Definitive stance: these eight are the additional non-duplicate findings I can substantiate from the provided artifact after excluding the already-known issues.
